Tools for Constructing and Testing Neuromechanical Models
6.1
Introduction: The Controller-Transfer Problem
A neural controller acts through the mechanics to which it is connected. Changing muscle
attachments, joint motion, inertia, or actuator behavior changes the mechanical response
to a command and the sensory signals returned to the circuit. A controller that produces
alternating motor activity can therefore fail to coordinate loading when transferred to
a different body. Investigating that transfer requires tools that make the mechanical
assumptions, neural computations, and exchanged signals accessible to inspection and
controlled testing.
An early experiment illustrated this problem. For a course project in ME 610: Neurome-
chanical Modeling, Morrow and I coupled the bipedal mechanics of Li et al. [2017] with the
two-level central pattern generator (CPG) of Deng et al. [2019] in AnimatLab [Cofer et al.,
2010]. The model included bilateral thigh, shank, foot, and toe segments, sagittal-plane
joints, and antagonist Hill-type muscles. I added a passive toe joint. A shared rhythm
generator (RG) supplied pattern-formation (PF) and motor-neuron (MN) pathways on
both sides. We adjusted currents, synaptic weights, and muscle parameters manually and
presented the suspended result at the NIH BRAIN Initiative Investigators Meeting [Bolen
and Hunt, 2021]. The legs cycled when suspended, but the model lost support when
released toward the ground (Figure 6.1). The continued neural rhythm did not establish
an effective load-bearing controller.

This experience exposed a practical gap between assembling a neuromechanical model
and using it to investigate control. Manual tuning made it difficult to isolate a faulty path-
way, distinguish a mechanical error from a neural error, or reproduce a useful condition.
Graphical construction could make circuits easier to inspect, while scripted execution
could make parameter searches and repeated experiments practical. Both required ex-
plicit command and sensory interfaces, checked model mechanics, and evaluation criteria
appropriate to the task.
This chapter addresses the fourth dissertation objective by developing tools for con-
structing and testing coupled neural and mechanical models. The methods connect
OpenSim- and CAD-derived mechanics, graphical neural construction, actuator and sen-
sory interfaces, staged calibration, and automated experiments. The results proceed from
mechanical and circuit checks to coupled responses, controlled interventions, and com-
putational performance. OpenSim, MyoConverter, MuJoCo, SNS-Toolbox, Simulink, and
Simscape provide the existing software foundations [Delp et al., 2007, Caggiano et al.,
2022, Todorov et al., 2012, Nourse et al., 2023]. My contributions are the model preparation

135
and repairs, editable blocks, actuator integrations, and experiment procedures that con-
nect those foundations. Appendix D gives supporting configurations, source scripts, and
secondary comparisons.
6.2
Methods: Constructing and Evaluating Neuromechanical Models
6.2.1
Workflow and Experimental Models
The workflow begins with a mechanical model and a control hypothesis (Figure 6.2).
Model preparation establishes the coordinates, actuator routes, force calculations, and
contacts through which neural activity will act. Controller construction defines the com-
putations performed by neural populations and the signals they exchange. Calibration
selects parameters for those functions, and physical evaluation tests the resulting coupled
behavior. Recordings then connect changes in the circuit to changes in movement and
loading. A failed test can require revising an earlier component before repeating the
coupled experiment.
Two complementary construction routes were developed. The human-model route
converts OpenSim mechanics with MyoConverter, checks and repairs the executable
model, and binds a named neural controller and actuator formulation. The graphical robot-
model route assembles CAD-derived mechanics in Simscape Multibody and connects
an SNS-Simscape controller. A separately assembled CAD MuJoCo model supports
additional experiments. The runtime bridge allows a Simulink controller to operate
MuJoCo mechanics; it does not automatically translate an arbitrary Simscape mechanism

6.2.2
Preparing the Mechanical Models
For the human-model route, I converted the Gait2392 reference from OpenSim to MuJoCo
with MyoConverter. The robot counterpart required separate preparation because its
artificial-muscle routes could not be combined with unchanged human-muscle parameters.
Biological-muscle actuators were retained in the human reference, while robot routes
and BPA forces were handled through explicit interfaces. The human model retains 92
actuator entries; six small hip-rotator entries remain disabled. The knee retains OpenSim’s
flexion-negative convention.
Mechanical checks preceded controller fitting. Single-actuator tests checked action di-

139
rections and force scales. Prescribed joint coupling and moving path points were inspected
over the intended range of motion. Contact definitions distinguished intended foot loading
from contacts involving other body parts or path markers. These checks matter because a
reversed action, erroneous force scale, or unintended contact changes the apparent neural
response. Appendix D.1 details the repairs and remaining force discrepancies.
The CAD route additionally required consistent anatomical frames, mass and inertia
assignment, joint topology, and actuator attachments. The robot frame uses x anterior, y su-
perior, and z right. CAD assembly placement was related to that frame through a reference
datum. The four-bar knees require their loop constraints to be retained in the dynamic
model. Moving and conditional muscle-route points require both geometric updates and
the corresponding force derivatives; changing a route’s length without accounting for
that dependence would give inconsistent generalized forces. Numerical derivative and
virtual-work checks test those relations before interpreting motion.
Model preparation also includes declaring the actuation approximation. The imple-
mented BPA interface evaluates the quasi-static force relationship from Chapter 3 at current
actuator length and commanded pressure, then applies tensile force along its route. This
calculation carries the measured static force dependence into a neuromechanical exper-
iment. Valve flow, pressure transients, and loading-history effects require additional
models and calibration. Biological tendon compliance and BPA series compliance are
likewise separate mechanisms. Selecting one of these implementations does not establish
the fidelity of another.

140
6.2.3
Constructing Controllers and Closing the Feedback Loop
The SNS-Simscape library implements neurons, chemical synapses, sensory encoders,
activation dynamics, and muscle-force elements as editable Simulink blocks (Figure 6.3).
It retains the conductance-based formulations used by SNS-Toolbox [Nourse et al., 2023].
Synapses supply conductance and conductance–reversal-potential products; the postsy-
naptic neuron combines these with its membrane state and other currents. Membrane
voltage and normalized motor command remain distinct signals. This organization permits
inspection of individual pathways and the calculations they perform.
The complete feedback loop connects MN output to activation or a pressure command,
the actuator model to tensile force, and the mechanical state to sensory encoding. Length,
lengthening velocity, and force provide inputs for Ia, II, and Ib pathways; foot contact
supplies a distinct event or load signal. Their encoding ranges, signs, saturation, and
update intervals must be stated. A synaptic conductance is not itself a sensory force, and
a normalized neural output is not a pressure until the command mapping defines that
conversion. Appendix D.1.3 records these interface distinctions.
SADb supplies the physiological context for selecting sensory pathways (Chapter 5). A
source record can motivate a homonymous, reciprocal, or phase-dependent connection,
but it does not uniquely specify its numerical gain in another body. The implemented
encoding and connection sign therefore remain part of the hypothesis being tested. Local
afferent pathways can act at MNs while additional pathways affect PF or RG activity. Their
effects must be established through the actual circuit rather than inferred from a sensory
label alone.

6.2.4
Functional Design, Neural Calibration, and Physical Curriculum
Functional design specifies what a neural pathway should compute before its parameters
are fitted. The specification includes the represented quantity, input and output units,
sign, operating range, temporal response, and saturation. For a PF channel, this includes
the intended onset, duration, and overlap of its transmitted activity. A channel’s flexor,
extensor, or synergy label does not establish those properties. Graded and spiking realiza-
tions require design relationships appropriate to their respective neuron formulations; the
equations and spiking calibration are given in Appendix B.
Neural calibration then selects parameters for these declared functions. I implemented
the four operations presented by Hunt [2019]: establish an intrinsic rhythm with a period
approximately twice the target locomotor period; tune entrainment using expected afferent
signals; fit feedforward motor recruitment; and refine the motor pattern with sensory feed-

143
back. Expected activation targets are inverse-mechanics estimates from reference motion,
rather than measured electromyograms. Their agreement with MN output measures the
stated calibration target, not biological validation of every neural pathway.
The physical curriculum evaluates the controller as mechanical demands change (Ta-
ble 6.3). Calibration can occur before and within these environments. Feedforward
recruitment is needed to observe meaningful deafferented motion, and afferent timing can
be fitted before closing the sensory loop. Fitting therefore supports the physical curriculum
rather than replacing it. The experiment drivers separately evaluate saved settings so that
advancement can be checked without changing the candidate during the test.

6.2.5
Automated Execution and Experimental Protocols
Automated searches use bounded parameter ranges and shared values for bilateral ho-
mologues where symmetry is intended. Tree-structured Parzen estimation proposes
candidates from previous evaluations. Each simulation records its settings, objective terms,
completion status, and acceptance measures. Saved configurations support replay in an
independent process before promotion. Failed trials remain informative because they
identify a limiting function or condition; a favorable numerical objective cannot substitute
for the required motion.
Acceptance begins with finite states, completion of the prescribed duration, and pro-
tected joint bounds. Suspended experiments assess meaningful joint excursion, cadence,
and bilateral phase. Ground tests additionally require unloading and whole-foot clearance,
contralateral loading, and a sufficient interval duration. Assistance is calculated from
recorded forces over a declared window. Vertical lift, horizontal guidance, and attitude
restraint are reported separately because reducing one does not remove the others. A
nominal support setting is therefore insufficient to characterize the loading experienced by
the model.
Controlled interventions hold the chosen model, controller parameters, drive, and sup-
port fixed while changing a specified pathway or applied stimulus. Continuous-current
noise, fixed parameter perturbations, and external mechanical pushes are different experi-

145
ments. Their units, injection sites, duration, and varied quantities are stated separately.
Aligned RG, PF, MN, joint, force, and support recordings permit a response to be traced
through the coupled system. Independent replays establish reproducibility under the
recorded implementation; local parameter checks examine a finite neighborhood around
that configuration.
Execution-time comparisons use the same named workload and distinguish complete-
process time from time spent in neural updates. Reference and accelerated calculations
are compared under matched inputs and model conditions before using the faster imple-
mentation for searches. Compilation, initialization, capture, and output can affect total
time, so a warm neural-kernel ratio is reported only for that kernel. Appendix D.6 maps
the relevant scripts to the tests and retained outputs.
6.3
Results: Verification and Representative Experiments
6.3.1
Mechanical and Signal-Interface Verification
Mechanical inspection exposed faults that would otherwise have been attributed to con-
troller behavior. Repairs addressed selected joint-action signs, active force scales, coupled
path-point limits, and intended ground contacts. At matched poses and OpenSim static-
optimization activations, eight of twelve sampled muscles had force-prediction R2 between
0.87 and 0.98 and mean forces within 10 % of the reference (Table D2). Rectus femoris
and biceps femoris short head had negative R2. Thus, the comparison identified useful
agreement and important remaining muscle-specific differences. It assigned pose and

146
activation frame by frame, without reproducing trajectory velocities or tendon dynamics,
and consequently did not establish dynamic equivalence of the muscle formulations.
Bridge tests established that a block-programmed controller could deliver muscle com-
mands and receive the corresponding measurements. Single-muscle activation, different
control rates, and sensor readback were compared with Python MuJoCo integration. The
five tested sensor arrays were bit-exact over 80 steps from 0.005 s to 0.400 s, excluding the
initial sample. A separate exported network drove all 92 actuator channels during a 5 s
run, and a closed-loop reflex experiment exercised both command and sensory return.
These results verify the interface operations under their stated conditions.
Circuit dynamics still required separate verification. One constant-drive Simulink
realization settled to a nonoscillating state while its NumPy reference oscillated. A larger
export agreed during an early transient and later diverged. These findings distinguish
successful signal exchange from successful transfer of a tuned circuit’s dynamics. Ap-
pendix D.2 retains the implementation comparisons and their limits.
6.3.2
Matched Circuit Calculations and Reflex Responses
The contact-driven W2L comparison tested a representative 26-neuron Simulink rhythm
core against the corresponding signals of the 95-neuron NumPy network. The core used
corresponding neuron parameters and shared pathways under identical drive and pre-
scribed heel inputs. Over the post-startup 2 s to 12 s window, burst periods matched at
1.000 s and all ten expected bursts were reproduced. Best-lag correlation of the four shared
RG voltage traces was at least 0.99996, allowing a 2 ms relative alignment lag (Figure D1).

147
Removing the phasic heel input caused both realizations to latch. This verifies the tested
shared rhythm core and input dependence, rather than complete-network or unshifted
sample agreement.
Reduced reflex models then tested the closed loop. The knee example contains homony-
mous Ia excitation, reciprocal Ia inhibition, and homonymous Ib inhibition for each antag-
onist, giving six feedback connections (Figure 6.4). A 2 nA, 30 ms pulse at the extensor Ia
sensory input produced 1.09˝ of extension, peaking 111 ms after onset. The response met
the specified recovery thresholds after 6.355 s. Broadened MN and Ia saturation ramps
produced this graded transient; the earlier narrow ramps maintained oscillations. The
actuators in this reduced knee test use the simplified linear BPA-force element. It is a
numerical circuit-response test, not a physiologically calibrated tendon tap or validation
of the complete Festo force surface.
In the loaded-cup experiment, the arm sagged by 2.00˝ with feedback enabled, com-
pared with 7.85˝ when disabled, at the 10 s endpoint of the loading ramp (Figure 6.5).
The applied mass reaches 0.625 kg at that endpoint; the comparison is not an equilibrium
measurement. Biceps stretch excites its own MN and reciprocally inhibits the triceps
MN; each Ib pathway inhibits its homonymous MN. This example uses the BPA20 force
block and its stated command mapping. The matched loading comparison demonstrates
a corrective effect of these pathways in the coupled model. It does not establish human
reflex gains or measured pneumatic pressure dynamics. Appendix D.2.2 supplies the more
detailed numerical checks for the knee response.

Controlled Interventions and Intermediate Timing Checks
A historical fixed-controller W2L comparison tested the contribution of sensory return
to bilateral ground-contact coordination. With conductances, drive, and support held
fixed, disabling the saved sensory-feedback channels shifted median bilateral contact
phase from 0.498 to 0.223 cycles. The accepted interval was 0.35–0.65 cycles, centered
on antiphase. Joint cycling and forward displacement persisted: displacement over 4.5 s
to 30 s was 2.239 m with feedback and 1.996 m without it. The retained evaluator also

153

baseline was not established by this pair. The result identifies a contribution to contact
coordination under those matched inputs, rather than a requirement for all rhythmic
movement (Figure 6.7). Additional pathway controls are retained in Appendix D.4.2.

Intermediate verification exposed a different limitation in the s3k and syn6 human-
model controllers. Their offline MN-output fits could satisfy an activation-error criterion
without reproducing the intended PF timing. In syn6, none of twelve channels passed the
combined provisional timing checks. Actual PF activity required three components per
side to explain 99 % of centered variance, compared with six for the intended primitives,
and one channel remained active throughout the cycle. The corresponding s3k activity
required two components per side, while quantitative intended PF windows had not been
declared. These are descriptions of the measured signals, not minimum neuron counts.
A bounded syn6 gain-only repair improved its fitting loss but still passed none of the
twelve channel checks. Subsequent RG-triggered relays and native SNS timing circuits
addressed the failed function directly. The native circuit passed all 48 channel-cycle checks
at the nominal cadence, and adaptive clocks extended that result to six controlled replay

6.4
Discussion
6.4.1
Contribution to Neuromechanical Experimentation
The developed tools make construction, calibration, and investigation of a coupled model
part of a reproducible process. Mechanical checks establish how forces act; editable
neural blocks expose the calculations and pathways; explicit interfaces connect those
computations to movement and sensory return. Automated drivers then support bounded
fitting and controlled experiments. Their value follows from the questions they permit
a researcher to ask: whether a force discrepancy precedes controller tuning, whether a
pathway changes timing or recruitment, and whether a selected result survives replay
under its recorded conditions.

160
The evidence is cumulative. Matched circuit calculations test implementation, the
reduced reflex models test closed-loop transmission, and the air and ground demonstra-
tions test selected coupled configurations. The original PF timing failure shows that the
workflow can identify an unsuccessful design even when a downstream output fit appears
acceptable. Later timing repairs also show that an accepted intermediate computation can
lose its intended behavior when live sensory return replaces prescribed replay inputs. This
supports the dissertation objective of developing research tools rather than treating one
visually favorable movement as the sole outcome.
Graphical and scripted environments serve complementary purposes. A readable
circuit can reveal an unexpected sign or shared input; automated execution can deter-
mine whether changing that connection affects the declared behavior over many trials.
Neither eliminates the need for the other. The current contribution is the demonstrated
integration and experiment procedures built on established software and published neural
formulations, with model-specific preparation and evaluation made explicit.
6.4.2
Interpreting Controller and Mechanical Evidence
Implementation agreement, functional response, and biological validation answer different
questions. Agreement under matched inputs establishes that a calculation was reproduced
for those inputs. A corrective reflex response establishes the behavior of the implemented
loop. Resemblance to biological organization motivates the model, but quantitative phys-
iological validation would additionally require appropriate measured targets, sensory

161
conditions, and perturbations. The inverse-mechanics activation targets and engineering
acceptance thresholds used here have narrower purposes.
Support conditions are equally important to interpretation. Air motion tests coordi-
nation without foot loading; supported ground tests introduce contact while retaining
specified assistance. Vertical support, lateral guidance, and attitude restraint each alter
the mechanical task. The coupled controller-transfer demonstrations reported here do not
establish harness-free walking. The current BiW2Lvar+ air stages, historical W2L feed-
back comparison, newer W2L108 ground result, and CAD hybrid-control result therefore
demonstrate complementary capabilities without forming one continuous curriculum
completed by a single controller.
The actuator formulation also changes the scientific question. Biological muscles,
ideal reference tensions, and quasi-static BPAs provide different relations among neural
command, force, length, and sensory feedback. The characterized BPA force surface gives
an experimental basis for static force generation, but it cannot establish valve response or
dynamic hysteresis. The simplified knee-reflex actuator isolates circuit response, whereas
the cup example exercises the BPA20 block. Those distinctions permit targeted verification
before a more detailed actuator model is used in a full-body controller.
6.4.3
Requirements for Further Integration
The immediate controller requirement is to verify the intended transformations at each
neural layer before optimizing the body response. PF channels need declared timing
windows and measured transmission, followed by motor recruitment and physical-stage

162
checks. Full-body postural control then needs to be integrated and tested with locomotor
commands under explicit mode transitions. A successful isolated postural circuit or an
earlier supported controller provides useful evidence for that work, but cannot establish
its completed outcome.
Mechanical fidelity requires equally focused development. Remaining muscle-force dis-
crepancies need matched dynamic comparisons with stated velocities, activation histories,
and tendon assumptions. BPA pressure and loading-history models need dynamic mea-
surements before their parameters can be interpreted physically. CAD routes, contacts, and
allowable joint motion must continue to be checked when the geometry changes. These
requirements connect controller testing to the actuator characterization and joint-design
studies rather than assuming that neural retuning can compensate for every mechanical-
model error.
Hardware transfer adds sensor calibration, communication timing, valve behavior, and
measured end-to-end latency. The existing embedded-interface scaffold supplies orga-
nizational elements for sensory encoding, command exchange, and watchdogs, but the
compiled SNS binding and physical I/O integration remain incomplete (Appendix D.6.1).
The simulation tools provide the model identities, signal definitions, and controlled tests
needed to approach those experiments. Chapter 7 considers their integration with mechan-
ical design and sensory evidence in the broader robot program.

163
6.5
Chapter Conclusion
This chapter developed and verified components for preparing mechanical models, con-
structing neural controllers, exchanging actuator and sensory signals, and conducting
repeatable neuromechanical experiments. Matched calculations, reduced reflex responses,
staged air motion, supported-ground examples, and recorded failures establish the capa-
bilities and current limits of those tools. Together they provide an experimental basis for
investigating how neural pathways, actuator behavior, and mechanical design interact,
and for extending that investigation toward the physical biomimetic robot.
